canonical_topic: Combustion as a bond-breaking oxidation reaction
definition: Combustion is described as an oxidation reaction in which existing chemical bonds in a fuel are broken and replaced with oxygen bonds; because oxygen bonds are generally lower-energy than the bonds they replace, this exchange is exothermic and releases heat.
core_idea: Fuels burn by breaking their internal chemical bonds (e.g., carbon-carbon or carbon-hydrogen) and forming new bonds with oxygen, and it is this bond-replacement process that releases the heat used for useful work like power generation.
key_points: Replacing most chemical bonds with oxygen bonds is exothermic, releasing heat as the byproduct that combustion harnesses.
Example: burning coal breaks carbon-carbon bonds and forms carbon-oxygen bonds.
Methane (CH4) has four carbon-hydrogen bonds; combining methane with oxygen breaks these bonds and produces heat, carbon dioxide, and water.

Most combustion needs an initial energy input (e.g., a spark) to break the first bonds; if the resulting heat is sufficient to break further bonds, the reaction becomes self-sustaining until fuel is exhausted.

A substance is combustible only if it has bonds that can be profitably replaced by oxygen bonds; water (H2O) is not combustible because breaking one hydrogen-oxygen bond to form another yields no net energy gain, regardless of temperature.
relationships: Explains mechanistically why carbon dioxide and water are unavoidable combustion byproducts, as described in the pollution-sources item.
trading_implications: Reinforces why CO2 output scales with the amount of carbon-based fuel combusted, a basic driver behind fuel-switching and emissions-intensity comparisons across generation types.
caveats: Combustion isn't just 'fuel catching fire' — it specifically requires bonds whose replacement with oxygen bonds is energetically favorable; not every substance that contains oxygen-linkable atoms (e.g., water) can sustain combustion.
